result.summary: Fragments describe the Cercopes, two knavish brothers named Passalus and Acmon, whose mother warned them to avoid Heracles ("Black-bottom"). Another tradition makes them children of Theia and Ocean who were turned to stone for trying to deceive Zeus.

scenes.title: The Cercopes and their tricks
scenes.summary: The Cercopes are introduced as cunning brothers who roam the world deceiving people. Their mother warns them about Heracles, and a variant says they were turned to stone for deceiving Zeus.
scenes.stakes: The brothers risk punishment for their trickery, from Heracles or from Zeus.

alias_notes.explanation: A nickname for Heracles, glossed in the text, used in the warning to the Cercopes.
The name for the pair, said to come from their cunning doings; it covers Passalus and Acmon.

notable_quotes.reason: Verse description of the Cercopes as liars and cheats.

analysis.text: The Cercopes embody trickery and hubris: those who cheat gods and heroes meet punishment, as the warning about Heracles and the petrification show.
The passage is a lexicon entry (Suidas) preserving fragments of lost early epic, showing how varied and contradictory the ancient traditions about the Cercopes were.

legacy.text: The Cercopes appear in later Greek art, such as metopes at Selinus, carried upside down by Heracles, and Greek words for knavery derive from their name.

fun_facts.text: The text comes from Suidas, a Byzantine encyclopedia of the 10th century, not from a surviving poem itself.

language_notes.text: Suidas, s.v.: the Suda, a Byzantine Greek encyclopedia; "s.v." (sub voce) means "under the word", so this fragment is quoted from the Cercopes entry.
Cercopes is explained as derived from Greek kerkos, "tail", and from cercopes meaning cunning or tricky deeds; the bracketed number is an editor's footnote marker.
"Black-bottom" is a nickname for Heracles, implying a hairy, sunburnt rear; the warning is that Heracles will one day punish them.
Turned to stone for deceiving Zeus: a variant myth, differing from the more familiar tale of Heracles capturing them.
"Irremediable" means incapable of being put right; their tricks cause harm that cannot be undone.

context_notes.text: Memnon was the legendary king of the Ethiopians, who fought at Troy and was killed by Achilles.
Theia was a Titaness, and Ocean the Titan who personified the great river encircling the world.

literary_notes.text: The mother's warning about Heracles hints that the brothers' trickery will eventually meet its match.
"Far over the world" and "continually" exaggerate their roaming to stress how widespread their deceit was.
